Article Title: An Idaho couple who have farmed beside a barbed-wire fence since 1979 fought the state over 5.95 acres, and an October 27 Supreme Court ruling reversed the state's title victory and reopened their own
Article Text:
Greg and Leah Sempel claim they used the disputed land for decades before Idaho acquired it in 1996. (AI image)

The disputed barbed-wire fence

How state came to claim the land

Couple refuse to give up land

What changed in Supreme Court

An Idaho couple who have farmed in Benewah County since 1979 have won another chance to claim 5.95 acres of disputed land after the state Supreme Court overturned an earlier ruling in Idaho's favour on Tuesday. Greg and Leah Sempel believed the land was theirs because an old barbed-wire fence had marked their property's boundary for decades. However, the state claims the land belongs to it and sued the couple in 2022 over its alleged unauthorised use.According to the judgment , the couple run Pokey Creek Farm, where they have grown crops, kept animals and built structures over the years. They say the land inside the fence was theirs because that was what they had been told when the property was purchased. They said the fence had been there long before they arrived, and they continued to treat it as the boundary.The state, however, has documents showing that the disputed 5.95 acres are part of a much larger property it acquired in 1996. But the Sempels argue that they had already been using the area for many years before the state became its owner. With the Supreme Court's latest ruling, the competing claim will be examined again.The story began in 1979, when Greg's parents purchased the property for him and Leah to use. Before the purchase, Greg said he walked around the land with Tom Rathbone, a representative of the company selling it. During that visit, Rathbone pointed towards a barbed-wire fence and told him it marked the northern boundary.Greg later spoke to Chester Henning, who had owned the property previously. According to Greg, Henning told him that the fence had been built in the 1960s after an agreement with the company that owned the neighbouring land.The couple say they had followed that boundary ever since. In their early years, they planted crops and kept horses in the area. During the 1980s, they harvested timber, laid a gravel access road and built several structures. In the following decade, they added a greenhouse and raised livestock.They also claimed that government workers carrying out logging operations had treated the fence as the dividing line between the properties.While the Sempels continued farming, the neighbouring property changed hands. It belonged to Milwaukee Land Company until 1981, when Potlatch Corporation acquired it. In December 1996, Potlatch transferred more than 4,100 acres to the State of Idaho through a land exchange. The disputed 5.95 acres were included in that transfer.Years later, a survey carried out in 2016 raised questions about the couple's use of the land. The state claimed that they were occupying part of its property without permission.In August 2022, Idaho took the couple to court. Apart from asking the court to recognise its ownership, it sought compensation over the alleged unauthorised use of the land, timber removal and property damage.The Sempels said they had been using the disputed area openly since 1979 and had treated it as part of their farm. They relied on a legal principle known as adverse possession, which can allow someone to claim ownership of land they have occupied for a required period, provided certain conditions are satisfied. The couple argued that they had met those conditions by 1984, long before the state acquired the property.They also maintained that the fence was not simply something built to keep animals inside. According to their account, it had been accepted as the boundary by previous landowners. The lower court, however, ruled in the state's favour on the ownership dispute.On the issue of property taxes, Greg said he and Leah had always paid taxes on their property, but the lower court found that they had not provided enough evidence to establish it. The couple challenged that decision in the Supreme Court.The Supreme Court found that the lower court had dismissed important parts of the couple's case without properly considering the evidence.For example, Greg had given a sworn statement saying they had paid their property taxes. Although older receipts were unavailable, the judges said that statement could not simply be treated as though no evidence had been presented.The court also considered whether taxes paid on the couple's recorded property could count towards the disputed area under an exception recognised by Idaho law.Photographs showed that some sections of the wire fence had become embedded in trees as they grew. The state argued that the fence was irregularly shaped and had fallen into disrepair. However, the judges said its present condition did not establish what it looked like when the couple first occupied the property or whether earlier landowners had accepted it as the boundary.For now, neither side has secured a final victory in the ownership dispute. The Supreme Court has sent the case back for further proceedings, where the couple's claims will have to be considered again.
Article Summary: Greg and Leah Sempel claim they used the disputed land for decades before Idaho acquired it in 1996. The state claims the land belongs to it and sued the couple in 2022 over its alleged unauthorised use. The couple run Pokey Creek Farm, where they have grown crops, kept animals and built structures over the years.

Article Title: A Nevada manganese mine that left arsenic and lead in the ground is undergoing an estimated $257 million cleanup; a 3.5-acre park has now opened on the former site, with more than 3,000 homes planned
Article Text:
Nevada mine site gets a new park amid $257 million cleanup and plans for 3,000 homes (Image Credit: Nevada Division of Environmental Division)

From wartime manganese production to an abandoned mining site

Why the cleanup carries a $257 million price tag

Greenbow Park brings a new public space to the former mine

More than 3,000 homes planned across 24 neighbourhoods

What was once a mining site associated with potentially harmful industrial waste is now making way for neighbourhood parks, walking trails and thousands of homes. In Henderson, Nevada, a former manganese mine that operated for decades and left behind contamination is being transformed into a large residential community. The opening of Greenbow Park marks a new phase in that redevelopment. According to the Nevada Division of Environmental Protection (NDEP), the Three Kids Mine site has been the subject of extensive environmental assessments and a cleanup programme, with the estimated remediation cost reaching approximately $257 million.The Three Kids Mine has a history dating back more than a century. Manganese ore was discovered at the site in Clark County, Nevada, in 1917. However, mining operations took place intermittently, including between 1942 and 1943 and again from 1953 to 1961. Manganese was an important industrial mineral, particularly during World War II, when demand increased for materials used in military equipment and steel production. According to the NDEP, an on-site processing mill was constructed in 1942 to meet the renewed demand for manganese during World War II.The mill reopened in 1951, and mining resumed in 1953. Mining continued until the open pits were exhausted, and operations permanently stopped in 1961.The end of mining, however, did not mean the end of the site's environmental problems. Former mine features included open pits, waste rock, an ore yard, processing facilities and tailings ponds. Environmental assessments identified dust, residues and processing waste containing lead, arsenic, manganese and petroleum. The contamination raised concerns about the condition of the land and the work needed before it could be considered suitable for redevelopment.The scale of the environmental work is reflected in the estimated cost. The NDEP's November 2023 Record of Decision placed the total estimated cleanup cost at approximately $257.5 million. The wider Three Kids Mine property covers around 1,165 acres, although the former mining operations affected a smaller portion of the site. The area affected by the former mining operations covered approximately 410 acres, distinguishing the contaminated mine area from the larger property earmarked for redevelopment. Environmental investigations and feasibility studies were undertaken to identify contaminants and determine the appropriate remediation measures.The federal Three Kids Mine Remediation and Reclamation Act was enacted in July 2014, creating a framework for transferring federally owned land through the City of Henderson Redevelopment Agency so that assessment, remediation and reclamation could take place. The land transfer was completed in February 2024, while major cleanup activities began in May 2024. The NDEP also established a perimeter air monitoring plan to monitor air quality during the work.The contamination identified at the site was not limited to lead and arsenic. Investigations also identified manganese, petroleum-related materials and other industrial waste. The environmental work therefore involved addressing several types of contamination rather than simply clearing away the remains of the old mine.One of the most visible signs of the transformation is Greenbow Park, a new 3.5-acre recreational space that has opened on the former mine property. According to FOX5 Vegas, the park is part of the Aries master-planned community in Henderson. Its facilities include pickleball courts, playgrounds, shaded gathering areas and more than 3,000 feet of trails. Visitors can also enjoy views of the Las Vegas skyline from the walking routes.The park adds recreational space to an area being developed into a residential neighbourhood. Its opening is significant because the former industrial property is now being incorporated into a community designed around housing, outdoor activities and shared public spaces. Rather than leaving the former mining land as an isolated industrial site, the redevelopment is intended to give it a new role in Henderson's expanding urban landscape.Greenbow Park is part of a much larger development plan. The Aries master-planned community is expected to include more than 3,000 homes spread across 24 residential neighbourhoods. The redevelopment covers more than 1,100 acres, making it a substantial addition to Henderson's residential growth. The community is being developed on the former Three Kids Mine property, with housing and recreational facilities planned as part of the wider project.The transformation also highlights the challenges involved in bringing previously industrial land back into urban use. Former mining properties can offer substantial redevelopment opportunities, but their conversion requires careful environmental assessment, remediation and long-term planning. There is also an important distinction between the progress of the redevelopment and the environmental project's official status. While Henderson's redevelopment director told the Las Vegas Review-Journal that remediation work had been completed, the NDEP's public project page continues to describe the overall cleanup as ongoing and lists site closure reports and monitoring documents.For Henderson, the opening of Greenbow Park offers a visible glimpse of what the former mine site could become. A property once associated with manganese production and industrial contamination is gradually taking on the appearance of a residential community, with parks, trails and thousands of homes planned as part of its next chapter.
Article Summary: Greenbow Park is part of a much larger development plan. The Aries master- planned community is expected to include more than more than 3,000 homes spread across 24 neighbourhoods. The community is developed on the former Three Kids Mine property in Henderson, Nevada. Environmental assessments identified dust, residues and processing waste containing lead, arsenic, manganese and petroleum. The cleanup cost is estimated at $257 million.

Article Title: 'Will be game over for America': Elon Musk raises three 'concerns' against Democrats ahead of midterms
Article Text:
Musk urged people to vote for Republicans

Musk's millions for Republicans

Why are the 2026 midterm elections crucial?

Billionaire entrepreneur Elon Musk backed Republicans on Friday and warned that a Democratic sweep of the US House of Representatives, Senate and presidency in 2028 could lead to what he described as the “end of democracy in any meaningful sense of the word”, ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.In a series of posts on X on Thursday, Musk outlined three changes he fears Democrats could pursue if they gain control of the White House and both chambers of Congress: granting statehood to Washington DC and Puerto Rico, legalising people living in the US illegally, and expanding the Supreme Court.“My biggest concern is that if there is a clean sweep by Democrats of the House, Senate and Presidency in 2028, they will,” Musk wrote, before listing the three possibilities as:1. Make DC and Puerto Rico states to gain a strong majority in the Senate.2. Open the borders and legalize everyone living in America illegally to cement a permanent majority.3. Increase the size of the Supreme Court to gain an immediate majority.He then added: “It would be game over for America.”Musk argued that the changes would allow Democrats to consolidate their political power and turn the US into a “permanent one-party state”. He called on voters to ensure Republicans retain at least 51 Senate seats in 2029, saying: “That is why you should vote for Republican senators this election.Other reasons are irrelevant compared to this one.”His remarks come just days before the US midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress for the final two years of President Donald Trump's term. Republicans currently hold narrow majorities in both chambers, but Democrats are seeking to regain control amid voter concerns over inflation, the economy and the administration's policiesThe billionaire's warning comes amid a broader political battle over the balance of power in Washington. Statehood proposals for Washington DC and Puerto Rico, immigration policy and the possibility of expanding the Supreme Court have been subjects of political debate, with significant disagreement between the two parties.Musk has emerged as one of the biggest financial backers of Republicans in the 2026 midterm elections. The Washington Post reported on October 23 that he had contributed about $446 million to influence the election cycle, largely through Republican-aligned political action committees.His contributions include substantial funding for the Senate Leadership Fund, which supports Republican Senate candidates, and America PAC, his own political action committee. He has also backed efforts to help Republicans retain control of the House.The spending marks a renewed push by Musk to influence US politics after his public falling-out with Trump last year.The November 3 elections will determine which party controls the House and Senate for the final two years of Trump's presidency. A change in control could significantly affect the administration's legislative agenda, spending negotiations and congressional oversight.Republicans hold a narrow majority in the House and a 53-47 advantage in the Senate. Democrats need net gains in both chambers to take control.Recent polling has favoured Democrats in the race for the House, while the Senate contest remains more uncertain. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted through October 26 put Democrats ahead of Republicans by 53% to 44% among likely voters on the generic congressional ballot. A CBS News/YouGov poll also projected Democrats on course for 229 House seats, although Republicans retained a narrow path to holding the chamber.The elections are being fought against a backdrop of concern about the cost of living and Trump's handling of the economy. A recent AP-NORC poll found that about 80% of voters identified the economy or cost of living as a major election issue.Even if Democrats win one or both chambers, their ability to enact major legislation would remain constrained by Trump's veto power and other institutional checks. A Democratic-controlled Congress could, however, intensify scrutiny of the administration and complicate its legislative priorities
Article Summary: Musk outlined three changes he fears Democrats could pursue if they gain control of the White House and both chambers of Congress. They include granting statehood to Washington DC and Puerto Rico, legalising people living in the US illegally, and expanding the Supreme Court. He urged people to vote for Republicans in the 2026 midterm elections.

Article Title: 'A win is a win': Israel opposition leader Lapid reacts to Netanyahu's poll setback
Article Text:
“It's not a knockout victory. It's a points victory. That counts too. A win is a win,” Lapid said (Photos: Agencies).

Israel’s outgoing opposition leader Yair Lapid, who is also the second most prominent leader in the B’Yachad alliance, has claimed that the anti-Netanyahu bloc “won” the election, even though it fell short of an outright victory. He called on the public to be patient while the bloc looks for ways to form a government.“It's not a knockout victory. It's a points victory. That counts too. A win is a win,” Lapid said.The anti-Netanyahu bloc took a combined 67 seats in the 120-member Knesset, but reaching a majority of 61 is difficult.Three of the four Jewish-led parties in the bloc (Yashar, B’Yachad and Yisrael Beytenu) have rejected the idea of sitting in a coalition with the predominantly Arab Joint List and Ra’am. The Times of Israel reported.Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ’s bloc won 53 seats, and his Likud party became the largest single party with 27. Still, Netanyahu also lacks a clear route to the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority.In a post on X, Lapid said that Netanyahu’s opponents had hoped for “a clear, immediate victory”, but maintained that the outcome should nonetheless be seen as a win for the opposition.“Netanyahu got 53 seats. A crash. Even from that small number, 13 seats belong to parties that declare they aren't Zionist,” he wrote, referring to the ultra-Orthodox parties United Torah Judaism and Shas, which won seven and six seats, respectively.“That leaves him 40 [seats],” Lapid said, contending that Netanyahu had no path to forming a government. “So we won,” he declared, calling the result “a win on points” instead of a knockout victory.Lapid said the opposition bloc, headed by Yashar chair Gadi Eisenkot, would use every means available to form a government, though he admitted the process would be hard and success was not assured.He requested “patience” from the public, explaining that forming a government is the opposite of an election campaign and happens behind closed doors, out of view of the cameras.“I know the human race hates uncertainty, but think how much you'd hate finding out in another month that for the sake of a headline or some leak, we didn't work smart, quiet, and precise,” he wrote.Lapid added that talks were taking place even though nothing had been announced publicly. “If you want to know if something's happening behind the silence you're hearing now, the answer is yes,” he said.
Article Summary: Outgoing opposition leader Yair Lapid calls on public to be patient while bloc looks for ways to form a government. “It's not a knockout victory. It's a points victory. That counts too. A win is a win,” Lapid said.

Article Title: Did Lacy misunderstand his Japan restaurant bill? Streamer reveals what actually happened
Article Text:
Image/Instagram

Lacy reveals why he thought he owed $12,000 at Japan restaurant

“Where I went wrong was not correcting the story once I found out,”

Lacy apologises to Japan restaurant after admitting he was trolling

“I never had bad intentions or intended for the restaurant to receive any hate,”

Twitch streamer Nick “Lacy” has finally explained the controversy surrounding his reported $12,000 restaurant bill in Japan. After facing criticism online, Lacy admitted that a language barrier made him believe he had to pay the entire amount, even though he later learned he only had to cover the extra food that had already been prepared. He also admitted that he joked about the situation during his livestream instead of correcting his earlier comments. Lacy has now apologised to the restaurant for the unwanted attention it received.In a post on X on October 29, Lacy explained that he initially misunderstood what the restaurant staff told him because of the language barrier. He believed he was responsible for a bill worth around $12,000.According to Lacy, he even told the restaurant that he would cover the amount and asked the staff to give the extra food to families. Since his livestream had been interrupted, he left his assistant to handle the situation so he could return to streaming.However, things changed when he came back online. Still frustrated and believing he owed the full amount, Lacy started talking about the incident and joking about it with his viewers.He later discovered that he only had to pay for the extra food that had already been prepared, rather than the entire bill.Lacy admitted that he should have corrected his story after learning what had actually happened.he wrote on X.He also admitted that he thought the situation was funny and never expected his comments to spread so widely online.Lacy also addressed the criticism he received after his comments went viral. He said he was not concerned about the hate directed at him but was worried about the effect his statements could have on the restaurant.Lacy explained.He also made it clear that the restaurant staff were not responsible for what happened. Instead, he accepted that both he and the people who placed the extra food orders were responsible for the situation.The streamer further revealed that he had reached out to the restaurant to make things right. He apologised for not explaining the situation sooner and for the unwanted attention his comments brought to the business.The controversy began during Lacy's October 28 livestream from Japan, when viewers reportedly used a QR code connected to his table to place extra food orders.While the incident quickly became a major talking point online, Lacy's latest statement has given viewers a clearer picture of his side of the story. He has now accepted that failing to correct his earlier comments was his biggest mistake.
Article Summary: Twitch streamer Nick “Lacy’ has finally explained the controversy surrounding his reported $12,000 restaurant bill in Japan. After facing criticism online, Lacy admitted that a language barrier made him believe he had to pay the entire amount. He later learned he only had to cover the extra food that had already been prepared. Lacy has now apologised to the restaurant for the unwanted attention it received.

Article Title: Brittany Mahomes helped raise over $200,000 for food allergy charity in 2023, now a project she launched with Patrick has its first approved Kansas City restaurant, with trained staff and strict kitch
Article Text:
Patrick Mahomes and Brittany Mahomes (Instagram)

A personal mission becomes public action

Patrick and Brittany Mahomes with their 3 kids. (Instagram)

What 15 and FARE requires from restaurants

Food allergy (Representative image)

Strict kitchen rules behind the recognition

A broader effort for Kansas City

Brittany Mahomes has spent years turning her family’s personal experience with food allergies into practical support for other families, and that work is now producing a visible change in Kansas City restaurants. In 2023, she helped launch a GivingTuesday fundraising match campaign with FARE, the Food Allergy Research and Education organization, raising more than $200,000 for food allergy programs. The following year, she and Patrick Mahomes’ 15 and the Mahomies Foundation formalised its commitment by partnering with FARE to create 15 and FARE, an initiative designed to make dining out, community food access, and everyday life safer for people living with food allergies. That initiative has now reached an important milestone. Joe’s KC has become the first Kansas City area restaurant recognised under the 15 and FARE program, with all of its locations receiving the designation, according to KCTV5. Customers can look for a “15 and FARE approved” sign at the restaurant, a signal that staff have completed extensive training and that the kitchen follows specific procedures to reduce the risk of accidental allergen exposure. For families who often approach restaurant menus with anxiety, the recognition represents more than a plaque on a door. It is an attempt to make a routine meal feel safer and more predictable. Read on for more details about it here:The Mahomes family’s involvement is deeply personal. Brittany and Patrick Mahomes have two children with severe peanut allergies, and Brittany has spoken openly about the constant vigilance that food allergy families carry with them. In materials shared by FARE, she described food allergy as a life threatening disease that requires constant attention, noting that it affects 33 million Americans, including her own family. Her experience as a parent navigating emergency room visits, daily precautions, and the fear of an unexpected reaction has become central to the public face of the initiative.That personal connection helped fuel earlier charitable work.During GivingTuesday in 2023, Brittany Mahomes and OWYN, a brand known for protein shakes free of the top nine allergens, launched a fundraising match campaign for FARE. The campaign raised more than $200,000, and FARE later honoured Brittany with its FARE Champion Award at the 15 and the Mahomies Foundation Gala in Kansas City. FARE CEO Sung Poblete said at the time that Brittany’s willingness to share her family’s story had inspired thousands of food allergy patients and their families to keep fighting.The partnership announced in November 2024 took that fundraising momentum and turned it into a structured community program. 15 and FARE brings FARE Neighborhoods and FARE’s Food Allergy Academy training to the Kansas City area. The goal is not simply to raise awareness, but to equip restaurants, food banks, pantries, school staff, and community health workers with the knowledge and systems needed to respond appropriately when someone has a food allergy.Becoming a 15 and FARE Restaurant Partner is not a symbolic endorsement. According to FARE, participating restaurants must train 90 percent or more of their food service staff, conduct monthly on site audits for three consecutive months, create a written food allergy management policy if they do not already have one, and demonstrate allergen transparency on their menus. Recognition is valid for one year, which means restaurants must maintain their standards rather than treat approval as a one time achievement.The program is free for restaurants in Kansas City, Kansas, and Kansas City, Missouri. FARE provides training and resources to businesses of all sizes, removing a major barrier for smaller restaurants that may want to improve allergen safety but lack the internal expertise or budget to build a program from scratch. Families dining out are encouraged to look for the “15 and FARE Restaurant Partner” logo as an indication that the business has met the program’s requirements.At Joe’s KC, the impact of the training was immediate. Front of house manager Lane Dougherty told KCTV5 that the process was an eye opener, particularly in showing how even a tiny amount of an allergen can affect a person. The restaurant’s allergen list has expanded to two pages, identifying which menu items contain which allergens and flagging ingredients produced in facilities that handle allergens. The list covers wheat, gluten, milk, dairy, peanuts, tree nuts, egg, soy, shellfish, MSG, and sesame.The practical changes at Joe’s KC illustrate why formal training matters. When a customer mentions an allergen, the request is passed to a staff member at the front counter, who communicates with the sandwich maker or kitchen team. That employee then changes gloves and cutting boards before preparing the order. The restaurant also uses separate fryers, keeping breaded items on one side and gluten free items on the other. These are small operational details, but they can make the difference between a safe meal and a dangerous exposure.The restaurant’s experience also shows how hidden allergens can appear in familiar dishes. KCTV5 reported that Joe’s KC barbecue beans contain Worcestershire sauce, which includes shellfish and soy. That kind of detail is easy for a customer to miss and difficult to identify without clear staff training and transparent menu information. Dougherty said more customers are now asking questions, and staff are able to provide useful answers rather than uncertainty.For Brittany Mahomes, that shift in everyday restaurant culture appears to be the point. When the 15 and FARE partnership was announced, she said the goal was to ensure Kansas City families have access to the resources they need to manage food allergies confidently and safely. She emphasised that the work is not only about awareness, but about being ready to act. Patrick Mahomes added that food allergy reactions can happen at any time and in any place, and that families should not have to face those struggles alone.Joe’s KC may be the first recognised restaurant, but it is unlikely to be the last. The 15 and FARE initiative is part of FARE’s larger Neighborhoods effort, which was created to reduce inequities in access to care, support, and resources for people with food allergies in marginalised communities. In other areas where the initiative has operated, FARE reported a 25 percent increase in families visiting an allergist and a 38 percent increase in epinephrine prescriptions, alongside improved confidence among food allergic individuals in managing their condition.Kansas City is the seventh FARE Neighborhood, and the local rollout includes training for community food banks and pantries as well as restaurants. FARE and 15 and the Mahomies have also hosted public education events, including a 2026 back to school event featuring an allergen free lunch demonstration, expert panel discussions, health screenings, and family activities. The initiative also includes access to FARE’s free online course, “Save a Life: Recognising and Responding to Anaphylaxis. ”The first approved restaurant gives the program a concrete example of what success can look like. It shows that allergen safety can be built into daily kitchen routines, staff communication, menu transparency, and customer service. More importantly, it offers families in Kansas City something they often struggle to find: a clearer sense of where they can eat with greater confidence.
Article Summary: Brittany and Patrick Mahomes have two children with severe peanut allergies. In 2023, she helped launch a GivingTuesday fundraising match campaign with FARE, the Food Allergy Research and Education organization. The campaign raised more than $200,000 for food allergy programs. The following year, she and the Mahomies Foundation formalised its commitment by partnering with Fare to create 15 and FARE. The initiative is designed to make dining out, community food access, and everyday life safer for people living with food allergies.

Article Title: Scientists examining 3,000-year-old bronze masks and ritual treasures in China found silk traces on 101 objects, with microscopic fibres and red pigment revealing how ancient people wrapped and colour
Article Text:
Textile residues adhering to artefacts excavated at Sanxingdui (Photos: Antiquity)

What the tiny fibres revealed

Red colouring found on the silk

Photographs of the eight sacrificial pits during excavation

Why position of the silk matters

How such delicate fabric survived

Scientists examining 3,000-year-old objects recovered from the Sanxingdui archaeological site in China's Sichuan Province have found traces of silk on 101 artefacts, including bronze masks, gold, jade and ivory objects. According to a study published in the journal Antiquity on Sunday, researchers used microscopic and chemical tests to examine the remains and found evidence that the ancient Shu people may have used silk to wrap or cover valuable objects during religious ceremonies. The tests also revealed traces of red colouring on some of the fabric.One of the objects examined was a large bronze mask with small patches of silk still attached near its right eye and eyebrow. Scientists identified three separate areas where the fabric had survived. Interestingly, the pieces did not all have the same weaving pattern or condition. This led researchers to consider whether different pieces of silk had been placed on the mask for decoration or as part of a ritual.The mask was among several objects recovered from Sanxingdui, a site associated with the ancient Shu culture. The objects belong to the Late Shang period, between 1300 and 1046 BC.Archaeologists have been studying the site for decades, particularly because of the large number of bronze objects discovered there.The first major collection of bronze artefacts was recovered in 1986, when excavations of two sacrificial pits produced more than 780 objects. Further excavations between 2019 and 2022 uncovered six additional pits. During investigations of these finds, researchers identified silk attached to several different materials. The latest study examined selected samples to find out what kind of fabric had survived and what its presence could reveal about the ceremonies performed at the site.Most of the silk remains were too small or damaged to be examined like ordinary pieces of cloth. Scientists therefore studied them under powerful microscopes and carried out chemical tests.Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) allowed researchers to examine the surfaces and shapes of the fibres. They found that the threads were generally smooth, with an average diameter of approximately 10 micrometres. Their shape closely resembled natural mulberry silk.The team then used Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) to study the chemical structure of the material. The results showed that the fibres contained proteins. By comparing these findings with the physical appearance of the threads, researchers were able to distinguish silk from animal hair.The examination also showed that the fabrics were not all made in the same way. Some were loosely woven, while others had tightly arranged threads. Most followed a plain-weave pattern, although more complicated weaving techniques were also present.When the researchers compared these fabrics with textiles from other Chinese archaeological sites of the same period, they found that some Sanxingdui samples had equally advanced or even higher weaving densities.Some samples contained coloured particles, prompting researchers to investigate how the fabric might have been coloured.In one sample, they discovered bright-red particles on the surface. Chemical analysis showed the presence of iron, while further testing identified the substance as ochre, a mineral pigment.Another part of the same sample contained calcite. Although this mineral is generally white, researchers believe prolonged contact with the surrounding soil may have changed its appearance. They also suggested that it could have been used as a coating on the silk.A different sample showed that instead of coloured particles simply sticking to the outside, a deep-red substance had entered the fibres themselves. The researchers believe this colour probably came from an organic dye.Finding silk on valuable objects was important, but its location inside the pits provided further evidence about its possible purpose.In two of the more recently excavated pits, the fabric was mainly found underneath the artefacts. Some objects also carried several layers of silk. A circular bronze ornament, for example, had as many as five identifiable layers.This arrangement led researchers to believe that people may have deliberately placed silk beneath or around objects during ceremonies.The researchers suggest that the material could have protected objects, covered them or formed part of the offerings themselves. Many objects deposited at Sanxingdui had also been broken or burned, adding to the evidence of ritual activity at the site.Silk usually deteriorates over long periods underground, but the conditions at Sanxingdui allowed some traces to survive.Much of the fabric had been preserved through mineralisation. As bronze objects corroded, copper and other metal substances interacted with the fibres, helping retain their original shapes.Not every piece survived in the same condition. Some had become carbonised, turning black and brittle, while others remained relatively well preserved. Researchers found that even different parts of the same sample could show different forms of deterioration.Although no systematic written records have been found at Sanxingdui, the researchers suggest that silk might once have carried writing or symbols. There is, however, no direct evidence confirming this possibility.Similarly, textile tools discovered at the site suggest that people were making fabrics, but scientists have yet to establish whether the silk itself was produced locally.
Article Summary: Scientists found traces of silk on 101 artefacts recovered from Sanxingdui. The objects belong to the Late Shang period, between 1300 and 1046 BC. The ancient Shu people may have used silk to wrap or cover valuable objects. Tests also revealed traces of red colouring on some of the fabric.

Article Title: Israel tightens airline security after flydubai hijacking
Article Text:
File photo: A flydubai plane parked on the tarmac

New screening measures

Israel has tightened security requirements for airlines operating flights to and from the country, requiring carriers to submit crew details 48 hours before departure, a month after an attempted hijacking of a flydubai flight exposed gaps in the screening of foreign pilots and airline personnel.The new directives, issued Thursday by Israel’s National Center for Passenger Data Analysis, apply to all incoming and outgoing flights operated by Israeli and foreign airlines. Carriers must provide crew information at least 48 hours before departure, submit any subsequent updates no later than two hours before takeoff and issue a final list at takeoff, according to The Times of Israel.The measures were ordered by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu following a security review and are intended to give authorities sufficient time to conduct background checks, Bloomberg reported.The changes follow an incident on September 30, when Omani copilot Hamam al-Hammami allegedly attacked Captain Smit Machchhar, the Indian pilot commanding a Flydubai flight carrying Israeli passengers from Dubai to Tel Aviv, and attempted to seize control of the aircraft. Despite being seriously injured, Machchhar managed to unlock the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew members to intervene and overpower the attacker.Two off-duty Flydubai pilots who were travelling on the flight subsequently took over the controls and diverted the damaged aircraft to Tabuk in Saudi Arabia, where it landed safely.Machchhar and fellow flydubai crew members were recently honoured by the UAE with the First Class Order of Zayed II for their actions during the incident. The award was conferred by UAE president Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, with the medals presented by Dubai Crown Prince Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum.The incident raised questions about how Hammami had been cleared to operate the route, particularly after reports that he had previously been grounded by Oman Air after extremist material was found in his possession.Israel’s Channel 13 reported that non-Israeli pilots, cabin crew and passengers travelling to or from the country will also be required to complete an online form 48 hours before entry. The forms will be reviewed by the Population Authority, while people arriving from countries designated as “red” will face additional scrutiny of entry forms and visa applications by the Mossad and Shin Bet, the report said.The Shin Bet, which previously oversaw security relating to Israeli airlines and provided security arrangements for flights departing Israel, will now also be responsible for procedures governing incoming foreign airlines and their overseas departure points.The changes follow reports of longstanding shortcomings in Israel’s oversight of foreign aviation security. According to Channel 13, airlines had been submitting crew lists shortly before departure, in some cases as late as 15 minutes after takeoff, leaving authorities little time to identify potential risks.A separate report cited an internal National Security Council document indicating that the Transportation Ministry had failed to fulfil responsibilities assigned to it for foreign airline security. The ministry had reportedly warned that it lacked the resources and operational capacity to carry out the duties, while an earlier warning in March 2025 flagged failures to comply with a cabinet directive on aviation security.The controversy also centred on access to passenger and crew data. Although the transportation ministry was authorised to access the National Center for Passenger Data Analysis’s database for aviation security purposes, reports said it had not taken the necessary steps to establish that access.Kan News reported that more than 1,200 crew members from countries without diplomatic relations with Israel, including Oman, Syria and Lebanon, had entered the country since the beginning of 2026. The figure has not been independently verified in the reports provided.The new rules are intended to close gaps in the screening process by giving Israeli authorities more time to examine crew information before flights depart.
Article Summary: Israel has tightened security requirements for airlines operating flights to and from the country. Carriers must provide crew information at least 48 hours before departure, submit any subsequent updates no later than two hours before takeoff and issue a final list at takeoff. The new rules are intended to close gaps in the screening process by giving Israeli authorities more time to examine crew information.

Article Text:
Two helicopters collide mid-air during flight near Oregon airport, three killed

Three people were killed after two helicopters collided mid-air near an airport in northwest Oregon on Thursday afternoon, according to the Yamhill County Sheriff's Office.The collision occurred around 2:15 pm local time near McMinnville Municipal Airport, about 40 miles southwest of Portland. Emergency responders, including local law enforcement, firefighters and medical personnel, rushed to the scene.One of the helicopters was carrying two people, a flight instructor from Texas and a student pilot from the United Kingdom, Yamhill County Sheriff Sam Elliott said during a news conference on Thursday evening. Article Title: A Virginia textile mill built in 1920 closed in 1996 and stood largely empty for decades; after a $110 million redevelopment, it now has residents and offices, with 190 apartments planned across the c
Article Text:
From textile production to a vacant industrial landmark

A $110 million effort to preserve history

Residents, offices and a new riverfront destination

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think about the redevelopment of the White Mill into Dan River Falls? A positive change for the community A good way to preserve history A necessary step for economic development 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

The 1920-built White Mill in Danville, Virginia, operated for 75 years before closing in 1996. Renamed Dan River Falls, the 650,000-square-foot historic complex is being transformed into apartments, offices, retail space and a riverfront community hub.A historic textile mill in Danville, Virginia, that once symbolised the city’s industrial prosperity has found a new purpose as a residential and commercial complex after decades of disuse. According to developer The Alexander Company, the former White Mill, built in 1920 and operated as Mill No. 8, is being redeveloped into Dan River Falls, a project valued at $110 million that combines 190 apartments with office space and retail facilities. The developer says the first residents moved in after the initial phase was completed in November 2024, while the redevelopment is scheduled for completion in 2026.The transformation reflects a broader effort to preserve Danville’s industrial heritage while bringing underused historic buildings back into economic and community life. The reinforced-concrete structure, which occupies more than 18 acres along the Dan River, is among the last surviving reminders of the city’s once-powerful textile manufacturing industry.Rather than demolishing the ageing mill, the redevelopment aims to retain its historic character while adapting its interiors for modern residential and commercial use.White Mill was built by Dan River Inc. in 1920 and began operating in 1921. Designed by Lockwood, Greene & Company, the five-storey building featured a simplified Gothic Revival architectural style and a distinctive reinforced-concrete structure. Its scale reflected the importance of textile manufacturing to Danville, where mills provided employment for generations of local families.The mill operated until 1996. As the textile industry declined, the building eventually stood largely idle, becoming a physical reminder of the economic changes that had reshaped the region. The decline of the wider textile industry cost Danville thousands of jobs, leaving former industrial properties struggling to find new uses.For decades, the White Mill remained a prominent feature along the riverfront, with the words “Home of Dan River Fabrics” once welcoming visitors arriving in the city. Its deteriorating condition presented a challenge: how could a vast industrial building be preserved without leaving it as an unused relic of the past? The answer came through a partnership between The Alexander Company, a Wisconsin-based historic redevelopment specialist, and the Danville Industrial Development Authority.The redevelopment effort began taking shape after years of discussions about how to reuse the property. In May 2021, Danville officials announced a partnership between the city’s Industrial Development Authority and The Alexander Company to convert White Mill into a mixed-use development. The original proposal called for 150 apartments and 110,000 square feet of commercial space in the first phase, with another 100 apartments planned for a later phase.Rehabilitation work began in December 2022. The project was subsequently named Dan River Falls, and the first phase was completed in November 2024. The developer's current plans list 190 apartments, 147,000 square feet of office space and a project completion date of 2026.The total investment is reported at approximately $110 million. According to Virginia Business, the redevelopment involved a public-private partnership in which The Alexander Company led the residential component, while the city and its partners oversaw commercial and public-facing elements. State and federal historic tax credits, alongside other financing arrangements, helped support the undertaking.The apartments are not the only sign of the building's return to use. By October 2025, 150 apartments in the first phase had become home to more than 275 people, and another 40 units were being made available. The developer also says the housing includes options for workers earning less than 80% of the area's median income, linking the project to local workforce housing needs.The former mill is also accommodating public offices and private businesses. In early 2026, Danville's Office of Economic Development and Tourism moved into the complex, joining the city's Parks and Recreation department. Engineering and consulting firm Dewberry also relocated its Danville office to the property.The project extends beyond the mill's walls. Plans include a riverfront park, an extension of the city's Riverwalk Trail and space for retail and other commercial activities. The developer's website describes more than seven acres of riverfront parkland as part of the wider development vision.Preserving the original structure while adapting it for new uses has been central to the project. The work retains the building's reinforced-concrete framework and historic architectural character while creating interiors suited to modern living and working. The redevelopment was also recognised by Virginia Business as one of the state's notable projects in 2026, reflecting the scale of the conversion and the partnership behind it.
Article Summary: The 1920-built White Mill in Danville, Virginia, operated for 75 years before closing in 1996. The 650,000-square-foot historic complex is being transformed into apartments, offices, retail space and a riverfront community hub. The developer says the first residents moved in after the initial phase was completed in November 2024. The redevelopment is scheduled for completion in 2026.

Article Title: US eyewear retailer accused of sharing customers’ prescription details and eye-exam activity with Meta as appeals court revives privacy lawsuit
Article Text:
Representative Image of the Eyemart Express website illustrating Meta Pixel tracking and customer interactions with prescription eyewear (AI-generated image)

Eyemart Express Meta Pixel lawsuit: what customers allege about prescription data, eye exams and Facebook tracking

Fifth Circuit ruling on Meta Pixel health data: why the court reversed the dismissal

What the Eyemart ruling means for online retailers and health data privacy

A US eyewear retailer faces a revived privacy lawsuit after a federal appeals court reversed the dismissal of claims that it shared customers’ health-related information with Meta. In Rand v. Eyemart Express , five Facebook users allege that a Meta Pixel tracking tool on the retailer’s website transmitted information about their prescription-eyewear searches, prescription details and eye-exam scheduling activity to Meta without their consent. A Texas federal court dismissed the case with prejudice, but on October 23, 2026, the US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reversed that decision and remanded the case for further proceedings. The court held that the customers had standing and had adequately alleged that their health information was shared with Meta, sending the case back to the district court to reconsider their claims. The ruling does not determine whether Eyemart Express violated any law. The court noted that the parties cited, and it knew of, no earlier circuit ruling on Pixel tracking of health information specifically.Eyemart Express operates physical stores and a website where customers can browse products, purchase prescription eyewear and schedule eye exams.According to the complaint, the retailer used Meta Pixel, a tracking tool that collects information about users’ activity on third-party websites and helps Meta build profiles for targeted advertising. The plaintiffs allege that the tool transmitted their website activity to Meta without their knowledge or consent. The five plaintiffs divide themselves into two groups. The Search Plaintiffs say they browsed the website for prescription glasses, triggering the Pixel to track their activity. One of them also alleges that, when she scheduled an eye exam, the tool sent Meta the name and location of the Eyemart store she visited. The Prescription Plaintiffs say they purchased prescription eyewear from Eyemart, entered their prescription information on the website and had that information shared with Meta.All five plaintiffs had Facebook accounts containing personal information, including their names and photographs. They allege that Meta could combine this information with activity tracked on Eyemart’s website to identify them and deliver targeted advertisements. They also allege that Eyemart uploaded customer lists containing email addresses and purchase information, including details of prescription eyewear customers had purchased or viewed, so Meta could match those records to Facebook profiles. The customers sued under the federal Wiretap Act, the Missouri Wiretap Act and the Illinois Eavesdropping Act. They also brought claims involving intrusion upon seclusion and breach of contract. These remain allegations, not established findings of liability. In reviewing the dismissal, the Fifth Circuit accepted the complaint’s factual allegations as true, as required at this stage of litigation.The panel was Judges Haynes, Higginson and Ho, and Judge Stephen A. Higginson wrote the opinion. The court first addressed standing, the legal requirement that plaintiffs demonstrate a sufficient personal stake in a dispute to bring it before a federal court. Eyemart renewed its argument that the customers lacked standing, but the Fifth Circuit agreed with the district court that the alleged unauthorised disclosure of individually identifiable health information constituted a concrete and particularised injury. It considered the alleged privacy harm comparable to harms recognised in traditional privacy claims. The court therefore held that the plaintiffs had standing to sue.The court then examined the two grounds on which the district court had dismissed the case. The first was that the Search Plaintiffs had not adequately alleged that they shared individually identifiable health information with Eyemart. The second was that the plaintiffs had not adequately alleged that their health information was transmitted to Meta. The Fifth Circuit disagreed on both points. It followed the parties’ approach of using HIPAA’s definition of individually identifiable health information as a framework for assessing the allegations. The court explained that such information need not consist solely of a specific diagnosis or prescription. Information relating to a person’s health or the provision of healthcare services may also fall within the definition when it identifies the individual.The Search Plaintiffs alleged that their searches for prescription eyewear and their interactions with eye-exam scheduling services generated information that the Pixel transmitted to Meta. One plaintiff alleged that the tool shared the name and location of the store she visited when scheduling an appointment. The court concluded that these activities could relate to the plaintiffs’ health and the provision of healthcare services. For the Prescription Plaintiffs, the district court had accepted that they shared health information with Eyemart by entering prescription details but found the allegations of disclosure to Meta insufficient. The appeals court said the lower court had focused too narrowly on sample illustrations in the complaint while overlooking other allegations about tracked product views, purchases, appointment details and customer-list uploads. Taken together, those allegations were sufficient to plead that the Pixel transmitted health-related information to Meta.The court stressed that, without discovery, plaintiffs cannot be expected to know much more at this early stage. It explained that a motion to dismiss tests the sufficiency of the pleadings, not the merits of the case. It did not rule that every element of each claim had been established. Instead, it reversed the dismissal on the two grounds it had considered and remanded the case, sending it back to the district court to reconsider the substantive claims. Discovery will be necessary if the district court finds that the plaintiffs have adequately pleaded the elements of their claims.The decision is limited to the issues addressed at the pleading stage. Eyemart Express can continue to contest the claims in the district court, where the evidence and remaining legal questions can be examined. Meta is not a party to this appeal, which concerns the retailer’s alleged conduct. The case also sits within wider scrutiny of tracking technologies used on websites dealing with health information. The US Department of Health and Human Services has published guidance titled Use of Online Tracking Technologies by HIPAA Covered Entities and Business Associates, outlining obligations for organisations regulated by HIPAA when using online tracking tools.That guidance has faced a legal challenge. On June 20, 2024, a federal district court in American Hospital Association v. Becerra vacated part of the guidance concerning circumstances in which an online technology connects an individual’s IP address with a visit to an unauthenticated public webpage addressing a specific health condition or healthcare provider. The Fifth Circuit noted that decision but distinguished the allegations in Rand, which involved claims that more extensive website activity was linked to identifiable Facebook users. The ruling may be relevant to retailers that sell healthcare-related products or facilitate appointments through websites using advertising trackers. Eyemart provides vision-care products and services, and the court said that activity on its website therefore pertains to customers’ vision.The decision is a pleading-stage ruling from the Fifth Circuit, whose jurisdiction covers Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi. It does not establish a nationwide rule that every visit to an eyewear website constitutes the disclosure of protected health information, nor does it determine whether Eyemart is ultimately liable. The next stage of the case will depend on the district court’s assessment of the plaintiffs’ substantive claims and, if those claims are adequately pleaded, the evidence obtained through discovery.
Article Summary: Eyemart Express operates physical stores and a website where customers can browse products, purchase prescription eyewear and schedule eye exams. The retailer used Meta Pixel, a tracking tool that collects information about users’ activity on third-party websites and helps Meta build profiles for targeted advertising. The plaintiffs allege that the tool transmitted their website activity to Meta without their knowledge or consent. A Texas federal court dismissed the case with prejudice, but on October 23, 2026, the US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reversed that decision.

Article Title: An Arkansas couple said their land was reachable only by boat across Beaver Lake or through a neighbour's property; they paid $8,000 for an 18-foot easement, but an appeals court upheld a route along
Article Text:
The Allens sought legal access across their neighbours' property to reach their land (AI image)

Road survey led to another dispute

Court supported the boundary route

What dissenting judge said

An Arkansas couple who paid their neighbours $8,000 for a road to reach their property have lost a court battle over where that road should be built. Connie and Delmar Allen could reach their land near Beaver Lake only by boat or by crossing their neighbours' property. Although both families agreed to an 18-foot-wide access route in 2023, they later disagreed over its location. On Wednesday, the Arkansas Court of Appeals upheld a decision requiring the road to follow the neighbouring land's boundary.According to the court judgment , the disagreement involved two families living next to each other in Benton County. The Allens owned land without direct road access, while their neighbours, Catherine and Jeffrey Wyant, owned property between the Allens' land and Old Bill Evans Road. The Allens wanted a permanent legal right to cross that land to reach their own property.The matter first reached court in March 2022. However, the neighbours managed to settle their differences before the case went to trial. Under their agreement, the Allens would pay $8,000 for an easement, which is a legal right to use a particular part of someone else's property. The Allens would also arrange and pay for a land survey to identify the route.The payment was made, and the Wyants signed the necessary document. What appeared to be a settled matter soon turned into another disagreement. The families had different views about where the road should pass, and the survey carried out after the agreement brought those differences into the open.The problem began with the route marked out by the Allens. Their proposed road would start at Old Bill Evans Road and run northwest across part of the Wyants' property.The Wyants, however, said they had agreed to something different. They wanted the road to run west along the southern edge of their land, rather than cut through the property.Both sides referred to the agreement they had signed in 2023. It included a simple drawing showing the neighbouring plots and a line marking the proposed access route. The document also said that a proper survey would be prepared later to give the road a more exact description.The Allens believed the final location could be decided through that survey, while the Wyants maintained that the original agreement had already established where the road should go.With neither side accepting the other's position, the Allens returned to court in February 2024. They complained that the Wyants would not allow construction to begin and asked the court to enforce the easement. They also sought to have their neighbours held in contempt for refusing to cooperate.The Benton County Circuit Court considered the different routes put forward by the parties. It ultimately selected the one running along the southern boundary of the Wyants' property and rejected the request to hold the neighbours in contempt.The Allens appealed, arguing that the decision was unclear. They also questioned whether the court had correctly interpreted the document granting them access.Their argument centred on the fact that the document called for a survey to establish the precise location of the road. They believed this gave them greater flexibility in deciding how to cross the neighbouring land.The appeals court found that the original agreement and the accompanying drawing already provided enough information about the intended route. It said that the later survey was supposed to add details, not allow an entirely different road to be chosen.Also, the Allens discovered that building the road along the southern boundary would be expensive because of the slope of the land and drainage problems. However, the judges said these difficulties did not invalidate the agreement.The ruling was not unanimous. Judge Brandon J Harrison disagreed with the majority and questioned whether, even if the Allens had a legal right to use the route, they could actually build a road there.In his dissenting opinion, Harrison pointed to a gorge measuring between 60 and 80 feet deep along the approved route. He argued that filling it would require considerable work and expense.Harrison also questioned the reliance on the original drawing. He believed it did not clearly identify an exact route and that the court should have considered whether the road would be reasonably usable for both families.Judge Stephanie Potter Barrett, who agreed with the majority, defended the decision. She said the dispute concerned an agreement the neighbours had already made, and the court's job was to interpret that agreement rather than select a more convenient route. The October 28 ruling thus leaves the Allens with their legal right to cross the Wyants' property, but only along the route approved by the court.
Article Summary: Connie and Delmar Allen could reach their land only by boat or crossing their neighbours' property. Both families agreed to an 18-foot-wide access route in 2023, but disagreed over its location. Arkansas Court of Appeals upheld a decision requiring the road to follow the neighbouring land's boundary.

Article Title: 1886: A New Hampshire family had an architect build 8-year-old Fanny a log playhouse with a working stove; it still welcomes visitors
Article Text:
AI-generated representative image showing the small nineteenth-century log cabin. Credits - Gemini

A summer cottage in the hills

Playhouses of the era

AI-generated representative image showing a cast-iron cooking stove and child-sized furnishings inside a nineteenth-century log cabin playhouse. Credits - Gemini

From playhouse to miniatures

Rich families on both sides of the Atlantic gave their kids something much better long before backyard trampolines and plastic play tents. They constructed tiny versions of actual homes. Throughout the late nineteenth century, playhouses proliferated on rural estates, and most were never meant to be simple toys. A youngster might exercise the adult skills of cooking, hosting, and managing a home on these small stages.One of the finest survivors is in the White Mountains of New Hampshire. Around 1886, a log cabin playhouse was built for eight-year-old Fanny Glessner at the family’s vacation estate, The Rocks, near Bethlehem, according to the Society of Architectural Historians . It included child-sized furnishings and a working cooker, and it still stands today, open to guests. It was created by Isaac Scott and used by Fanny to practise her homemaking talents, hosting tea parties and making jams and jellies.To understand why a girl in 1886 had a cabin like this, it helps begin by looking at her family’s summer traditions. Fanny’s father, John Jacob Glessner, was a Chicago businessman who later helped found International Harvester, according to the Forest Society . The family first came to the North Country of New Hampshire in 1878 because the mountain air helped her brother George’s hay fever.After a few summers in a big resort hotel, they bought land of their own. In September 1882 they bought their first 100 acres, and a year later their home, called simply the Big House, was finished. That mansion was planned by the same family friend, Isaac Scott, who would go on to create much of the estate. His buildings included a carriage barn, a gardener’s cottage, an observatory, various summer houses and a bee house for Fanny’s mother, Frances.Fanny's cottage was hardly the only theatre of the times. Playhouses and Privilege, a new book, examines children’s playhouses built on British and American estates from the 1850s to the mid-1930s. The story begins near the start of that saga, at Osborne, at the Swiss Cottage erected in 1853 for Queen Victoria and Prince Albert. A children's cottage on the grounds of Cornelius Vanderbilt's Newport house was erected in 1886, the same year as Fanny's. In Chicago, the Sears family also built a log cabin on Prairie Avenue in the 1880s, and it survives today in Kenilworth, Illinois.Fanny’s cabin was well used. The Forest Society now maintains it for The Rocks and recalls that she spent many hours there playing, baking and making jellies. It used to be atop the hill, close by the Big House. Fanny moved it down behind the cottage later. In 1999 the Forest Society moved it again to its present place, where it is open to tourists.The cabin’s most famous resident moved on to a career that, weirdly enough, was also about establishing little worlds. Fanny grew up to become Frances Glessner Lee, who is known today as a pioneer of forensic science. After coming into the family fortune in the 1930s, she turned to forensic science in her fifties. In the 1940s, she produced the Nutshell Studies of Unexplained Death, a series of highly realistic, miniature crime scenes to instruct homicide investigators, which the Smithsonian American Art Museum describes as a meeting point of craft and forensic science. In 2017, the museum showed all 19 studies thought to survive together for the first time at its Renwick Gallery.Fanny never really left The Rocks. Later she made the Gardener’s Cottage her home and in 1938 enlarged her cottage at The Rocks so that she could live there all year round. In 1940, she had a tea house and pond built in the gardens that had been laid out with the help of the firm of Frederick Law Olmsted. Meanwhile, her tiny crime scenes were constructed between 1943 and 1948, and for each she worked from case records and witness accounts based on actual investigations. No one knows if it was a log cabin in the forests of New Hampshire that gave her the idea. But a childhood spent maintaining a little residence, with its own cooker and sparse furniture, sits well with an adult existence of carefully crafted smaller spaces.Today, the playhouse sits on land that still functions as a Christmas tree farm. In 1978, two of the Glessners’ grandchildren donated The Rocks, by then around 1,400 acres with 22 buildings, to the Forest Society, with the proviso that there must always be a crop growing in the field. For decades, that crop has been Christmas trees. If you are planning to visit Bethlehem, you can view the cabin where an eight-year-old once baked and canned jellies, but you might want to verify the Forest Society’s guest information before you go.
Article Summary: A log cabin playhouse was built for eight-year-old Fanny Glessner at the family’s vacation estate, The Rocks, near Bethlehem, New Hampshire. It included child-sized furnishings and a working cooker, and it still stands today, open to guests.

Article Title: After 15 years in accounting, Linda Harrison left office work to raise fainting goats in Tennessee; 2½ years later, she called ranching her passion
Article Text:
AI Representation: After 15 years as a CPA, Linda Harrison left corporate office work to raise fainting goats in Tennessee. Image credits: Chatgpt

Why accounting no longer suited her

How the Tennessee farm began

Caring for livestock became part of Harrison’s daily routine as her small Tennessee farm grew into a goat-breeding business. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Caring for goats became part of her daily life

Ranching became her passion

A career can provide financial stability without necessarily offering the kind of everyday life a person wants. Linda Harrison, a certified public accountant (CPA), spent 15 years in accounting, as she explained in a 2007 interview with Brett Farmiloe’s Pursue the Passion project. Even so, she kept searching for ways to spend more time outdoors. Eventually, Harrison and her husband, Brian, decided to raise fainting goats on their land in Hermitage, Tennessee. In the interview, published on November 13, 2007, Harrison said she had been ranching for two and a half years, which places the start of her ranching experience around 2005. The change was gradual, though, as the farm grew alongside their careers and became a bigger part of their future.Harrison’s career began in public accounting as a CPA and later moved to contract jobs for various firms. Although contracting allowed for some flexibility, it could not eliminate the dissatisfaction associated with spending long hours indoors. Harrison enjoyed going jogging in parks during weekends or her off time. Being outdoors was very important to her and she was looking for ways of arranging her working life in a manner that would give her more opportunities to be outdoors.Another option she considered was learning botany, hoping that yet another qualification would give her a chance of working in her desired environment. At the same time, she was wondering if getting another degree would only bring her back to an office. Harrison did not plan to spend years saving up before quitting accounting. Instead, she looked into other alternatives, knowing that any new business idea needed its own financial justification.Harrison and her husband purchased property in Hermitage, Tennessee, while they were both employed. She started with a few sheep and miniature goats to cut down on the time and labor that was necessary for her to maintain her land. Over time, she realized that the livestock would become more than a method of clearing her property. Harrison and Brian began by breeding registered goats. Myotonic goats are called fainting goats because they stiffen and may collapse when startled, but they do not actually faint. The cause is a genetic condition called myotonia congenita, which the University of California, Davis, Veterinary Genetics Laboratory explains in its official guide to myotonic goats. As the herd grew, Harrison established a website to promote the animals and reach potential customers. This allowed the farm to attract buyers from beyond the immediate Tennessee market and helped turn a small livestock operation into a recognised breeding business.The management of the farm included some tasks aside from feeding the animals and searching for customers. Harrison was responsible for monitoring the goats and caring for them when they became ill. Harrison’s commitment was tested when she spent about three weeks nursing a single sick goat at home. This process required both time and money, which made Harrison wonder how much she should spend on a goat that would not be profitable enough. However, she felt responsible for the goat and took care of it. This situation demonstrates the dilemma that every livestock farmer faces: they must keep the enterprise profitable while also taking responsibility for the animals’ lives. Brian searched for the necessary information concerning feeding the animals, while Harrison did most of the work with the heart. According to her, their cooperation was complementary.Looking back on those first years of ranching, Harrison told Pursue the Passion in 2007, “Ranching is my passion and goats are my dream,” adding that she had never been happier. The excitement had seen her through the more boring aspects of farm life, such as the tasks in winter, taking care of the farm animals and making sure they had something to drink during the chilly season. All these were part of the work and not just interruptions to it. The 2007 interview with Pursue the Passion captures her reasons for pursuing ranching and the lessons she learned along the way. The tale told by Harrison is not just that of a woman moving out of an office into the open air. Rather, it is one of slowly constructing an alternative while knowing what she had been looking for in her career. Having spent 15 years in accounting, she discovered that she could marry her love for the outdoor life, caring for animals and her entrepreneurial spirit through goat-raising.
Article Summary: Linda Harrison worked as a CPA for 15 years in corporate office work. She and her husband decided to raise fainting goats on their land in Tennessee. Myotonic goats stiffen and may collapse when startled, but they do not actually faint. Harrison and Brian began by breeding registered goats.

Article Title: An Ohio man bought a house in a neighbourhood of about 140 homes and advertised it on Airbnb, arguing it was also his residence; on October 26, an appeals court upheld a zoning ban after neighbours ob
Article Text:
Rejection of primary residence argument

Growing legal precedent on short-term rentals

An Ohio appeals court has upheld a local zoning ban on short-term home rentals. The ruling shuts down a property owner’s attempt to run an Airbnb business in a quiet suburban neighborhood of about 140 homes. In a decision issued on 26 October 2026, the Fifth District Court of Appeals of Ohio backed a lower court ruling against home buyer Michael A. Clevenger. The court found that local residential zoning rules legally bar short-term tourist rentals run as a business in single-family zones. The dispute began after Clevenger bought a single-family house in a housing development of about 140 properties in Stark County, Ohio. Soon after he took ownership, he listed the house on online booking sites. He advertised it for short stays to passing guests and vacationers. Nearby residents quickly raised concerns about crowded parking, noise, and safety risks. Local zoning inspectors then issued a formal notice of violation. They said he was running an unapproved business in an area zoned only for single-family homes. Clevenger appealed the enforcement action to the local township zoning board.He then appealed to the Stark County Court of Common Pleas. He argued that renting out the house did not break the zoning code. He said the house was his main home and that he only sometimes hosted guests.The Fifth District Court of Appeals rejected Clevenger’s arguments one by one. It held that short-term commercial rentals change the basic residential character of a neighborhood. This is true even if the owner sometimes sleeps at the property. The court wrote for its three-judge panel that local township zoning codes exist to protect stable, quiet, low-density living for long-term residents. Court records show that neighbors gave local authorities logs, photographs, and testimony. These described frequent guest turnover, parties, and unfamiliar cars parked along narrow residential streets. The appeals judges decided that advertising a house for paid short stays turns a single-family home into a hotel-style business. That kind of business needs specific commercial zoning approval or a conditional use permit. The property had neither. The court also ruled that the local zoning board acted within its legal powers when it read the township land-use codes. It confirmed that local governments in Ohio have clear police powers to limit short-term rentals. These powers protect neighborhood safety and property values.The 26 October ruling adds to a series of similar decisions in Ohio state courts. Those decisions back the right of local towns and township trustees to limit or ban platforms like Airbnb and VRBO in established residential areas. Lawyers for local homeowners argued during court hearings that unmonitored commercial rentals in a subdivision of 140 homes would badly weaken deed restrictions and local land planning rules. Those rules are meant to build long-term community ties. Under Ohio law, township trustees have broad power to define land uses within set zones. Courts have repeatedly held that short-term rentals do not count as normal single-family residential use. This is because guests do not live there permanently or sign long-term leases. The decision makes clear that property owners cannot avoid local short-term rental bans by simply calling a property their personal residence while actively offering rooms to paying travelers. Clevenger can still ask the Supreme Court of Ohio for a discretionary review. However, state legal experts consider it unlikely that further appeals would overturn the settled precedent on local township land-use powers.
Article Summary: Ohio appeals court has upheld a local zoning ban on short-term home rentals. The ruling shuts down a property owner’s attempt to run an Airbnb business in a quiet suburban neighborhood of about 140 homes. The appeals judges decided that advertising a house for paid short stays turns a single-family home into a hotel-style business. That kind of business needs specific commercial zoning approval or a conditional use permit.
